earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog lists only subclassification comments (Edwards 2021; van Engelenhoven 2009); no grammar/phonology of Habu found online or named

sources.citation: Greksakova, Zuzana. 2018. Tetun in Timor-Leste: the role of language contact in its development. Tese de doutoramento (PhD thesis), Universidade de Coimbra. 442 pp. (Estudo Geral hdl 10316/80665, openAccess.)
sources.note: Nothing about Habun. The only prosodic statements concern Tetun Prasa (penultimate stress in native words, acute accent marking irregular stress in the INL orthography, Portuguese loans keeping original stress, after Albuquerque 2011) and Hull's tonic/atonic vowel terminology for historical Tetum; Habun is named once in a classification footnote.

sources.citation: Hull, Geoffrey. 2000. Historical phonology of Tetum. Studies in Languages and Cultures of East Timor 3: 158-212 (also van Engelenhoven & Hajek 2000 in the same volume).
sources.note: Tetum-centred; Habun cited only for segmental reflexes (*p > h 'shared today by Habun, Bekais, Kawaimina'; *b > [w] 'in North Atauran, Kawaimina and Habu'). Uses tonic/atonic/pretonic vocabulary but states no stress-placement rule, and none for Habun; p.158 says individual phonological studies of the other ten Timoric languages were 'currently in preparation by the author'.

sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026. The Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste: Unravelling their prehistory and classification. Berlin: Language Science Press (catalog book 526; Zenodo record 18323007, CC-BY 4.0, published 2026-02-21).
sources.note: Habun appears only in historical-phonology tables and prose : reflexes of PMP *j, *R, *ŋ, final *-ay/*-aw/*-uy, penultimate and final *schwa ('Habun has penultimate *ə > o before back vowels and penultimate *ə > e before other vowels'), *z > y, *b > w, all from Dawson 2014 forms. Nothing on Habun stress. The volume's only general stress remark is in the Flores/schwa discussion (ch. 3): 'While penultimate stress is the normal rule for Wallacean languages, words with penultimate schwa can have stress on other syllables' - an areal generalisation, not a Habun statement. 67 MB PDF downloaded unde…

sources.citation: Wikipedia (en) 'Habun language' and (de) 'Habun', downloaded 2026-09-17.
sources.note: Stub articles (classification, speaker numbers from 2010/2015 censuses, Hull's 'archaic variant of Tetum' remark). No phonology, no references beyond Ethnologue and census.

sources.citation: OLAC resources in and about the Habu language (language-archives.org/language/hbu), Internet Archive copy up-to-date as of 23 Jan 2025.
sources.note: Lists only: PARADISEC VD1-hbu20140210_wordlist (Habun wordlist) and VD1-hbn20140206_story (Dawson 2014), Glottolog, Ethnologue. No language description exists in any OLAC archive.

sources.citation: Culhane, Kirsten. 2024. The prosodic foot: A typological study of greater Timor languages. Inaugural-Dissertation (Dr. phil.), Philologische Fakultaet, Albert-Ludwigs-Universitaet Freiburg i. Br. (submitted SS 2023, defended 19.01.2024; supervisors U. Reinoehl, N. P. Himmelmann). vi+253 pp. DOI 10.6094/UNIFR/243922.
sources.note: Habun is analysed only phonotactically from Dawson's 226-item wordlist: five vowels /i e a o u/ with the co-restriction *high+mid vowel within a foot (Table 3.18, Table 4.8: 'Idate, Dadu'a, Galolen, Habun, Semau Helong'), evidence for right-aligned disyllabic weight-insensitive feet from 'distribution of vowel sequences, consonant clusters, vowel co-restrictions' (sec. 4.1.4 item f), 'Habun: insufficient data' on the footing of CC clusters (Table 4.16), Habun listed among GTLs with 'only phonotactic evidence for foot structure' (132g) and 'not well-described' (ch. 8 fn. 4). sources.citation: Klamer, Marian & Francesca Moro (eds.). 2023. Traces of Contact in the Lexicon: Austronesian and Papuan Studies. Leiden: Brill.
sources.note: Habun mentioned once in a classification list (East Timor group of Timor-Babar, after Edwards 2018). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Edwards, Owen. 2021. Rote-Meto Comparative Dictionary. Canberra: ANU Press.
sources.note: Cites Habun forms from Dawson 2014 (PARADISEC VD1 Manatuto survey) and notes *schwa > o in Tetun and Habun; nothing on Habun stress.

sources.citation: Schapper, Antoinette. 2020. [paper on Austronesian languages of eastern Timor, HAL halshs-02935746].
sources.note: Uses Hull 2001 as the source for Habun; discusses Habun subject-agreement prefixes (k- etc., occurring on both vowel- and consonant-initial roots). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Kaiping, Gereon A., Owen Edwards & Marian Klamer (eds.). 2019. LexiRumah 3.0.0. Leiden: Leiden University Centre for Linguistics. Lect 'habu1241' Habun (216 forms; Source dawson14 = Dawson, Virginia. 2014. Manatuto survey word lists, PARADISEC VD1; comment 'collected in Cribas'; orthography profile p/manatuto).
sources.note: Wordlist data only: Form / Segments / Local_Orthography columns (e.g. lorok_matan 'sun', wulan 'moon', udung [uduŋ] 'mountain', book [boːk] 'smoke', roo [roː] 'canoe', ni'in [niʔin] 'teeth', ha'a [haʔa] 'four'). Vowel length and glottal stop are transcribed; the 12 forms with apostrophes are all glottal stops; no stress or pitch marks in any of the 216 rows and no prosodic comment field. Not a statement; allows no inference on stress placement without the audio.

sources.citation: Dawson, Virginia. 2014. Manatuto survey (VD1): Habun wordlist (VD1-hbu20140210_wordlist) and story 'Tradisaun yala woun' (VD1-hbn20140206_story). PARADISEC.
sources.note: Only recorded Habun audio known (OLAC); would allow a first-hand determination of stress placement in citation forms if no printed statement exists.

sources.citation: Lewis, Simons & Fennig (eds.). 2013. Ethnologue, 17th ed., entry 'Habun' [hbu] (Internet Archive copy).
sources.note: Population 2,700 (2010), location NE of Laclubar, 'many loanwords from Trans-New Guinea languages similar to Makasae, but with Austronesian structure'. No phonology.

sources.citation: Hull, Geoffrey. 2004. The Languages of East Timor: Some Basic Facts. Dili: Instituto Nacional de Linguistica, Universidade Nacional Timor Lorosa'e (rev. 24.8.2004).
sources.note: Section '2. HABUN' gives location (Cribas district south of Manatuto), calls it 'an archaic variety of Tetum' close to Kawaimina and Idate, and lists numerals 1-10 (isa, rua, tolu, haa, lima, neen, hitu, ualu, sia, sanulu). Nothing on phonology or stress.

sources.citation: Albuquerque, Davi Borges de. 2003 [issue dated 2003, online 2010]. As linguas de Timor Leste: perspectivas. Lingua e Literatura (Universidade de Sao Paulo) 27: 313-335.
sources.note: Nothing. The Habun entry reads only: 'e uma lingua pouco estudada e possui um numero reduzido de falantes, cerca de 1200 falantes, segundo o Ethnologue (2009). Hull (2001a) considera-a uma versao arcaica do tetum'. No phonology anywhere in the article for any language beyond Tetum dialect remarks; a full-text search for stress/accent acento/stress/tonic finds nothing.

sources.citation: Esperanca, Joao Paulo Tavares. 2001. Inventario de fonemas do tetum, um olhar sobre a silaba e algumas questoes sobre reduplicacao. In Estudos de Linguistica Timorense, Aveiro: SUL, 48-90 (archive.org item 'ling_timor').
sources.note: Tetum stress rule only; Habun not mentioned.

sources.citation: Hull, Geoffrey. 1998. The basic lexical affinities of Timor's Austronesian languages: a preliminary investigation. Studies in Languages and Cultures of East Timor 1: 97-174 (+ appendix wordlists), in the INL 2001 reprint of vol. 1 (archive.org item dated 2004).
sources.note: Habun (abbrev. Hb., informant Aurelia Neves de Sousa, Cribas) appears in classification footnotes (fn.13: 'proper to the Cribas district'; fn.20: 'essentially an archaic variety of Tetum.. transition between Tetum and Kawaimina') and in the comparative wordlists (e.g. loro, ulan, tinan, rai, wai, ahi, noso). No stress marks, no stress statement.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 sources.bib (local CLDF dump), all entries with language code [hbu].
sources.note: Only two entries carry [hbu]: Hull 1998 (lexical affinities) and Hull 2001 (morphological overview, SLCET 4: 98-205). No phonology, grammar or sketch of Habun is registered.

sources.note: The only registered work containing Habun grammatical data (Glottolog's sole non-wordlist [hbu] reference; Schapper 2020 draws Habun morphology from it). Hull's overviews sometimes open with phonological/orthographic preliminaries; if any printed remark on Habun stress exists, it is most likely here.
